videos.summary:
Nate Herk compares Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol using the same prompts in his own workflow, with stated token prices of $4/$20 versus $2/$10 per million input/output tokens. An initial Fireflies retrieval test finds Sol faster early on but wrong about the latest relevant Q&A (August 17 versus Opus’s September 14); on a scroll-driven coffee-and-protein website he prefers Opus’s product imagery and layered animation, despite a roughly threefold higher task cost. These are his hands-on judgments, not general benchmark rankings.

In a 30-second promo assembled from roughly 100 GB of event footage, he finds Opus’s music, pacing and layering more persuasive; its Instagram edit also beats Sol’s hum-affected, sparse version, though neither reel is ready for his feed without more work. His sheets/deck/dashboard comparison cannot be scored: both agents edited the same repository, and a later audit revises the Sol run to about $3.60 and nine minutes. The same shared-file contamination invalidates the museum game comparison, where a mouse-lock bug makes the observed game hard to play.

In isolated 3D learning-world builds based on 100 prior videos, Nate prefers Opus’s interactive token/context-window activities to Sol’s cluttered interface, despite about $60 versus $8.55 and 1h45 versus 50 minutes. Opus also produces the better October trip-planning globe and includes San Francisco Tech Week, whereas Sol’s itinerary supplies links but misses the intended event emphasis. A separate code-repair test reverses the result: Nate reports Sol scoring 100/100 against Opus’s 97/100 for roughly $1 and around one-twentieth the spend, with a cybersecurity interruption and a revised prompt complicating comparison.

For a Skool course assembled through the browser, both models upload material and Opus is faster and cheaper despite duplicate links; for a Canva drawing from a reference image, Nate strongly favors Opus after Sol first substitutes a generated image and then produces poor drawings. His final score is seven Opus wins, one Sol win and two discarded tests; reported totals are about 8h40/$213 for Opus and 5h51/$74.46 for Sol, with his earlier cost correction worth remembering. His verdict is to favor Opus for creative work and judgment, use cheaper Sol for defined worker tasks or code repair, and isolate each agent’s files before treating side-by-side results as evidence.
videos.why_valuable: Helps choose between a premium creative/orchestration model and a cheaper coding worker for specific tasks, while showing why shared workspaces and corrected costs can invalidate a model comparison.
key_takeaways: 00:21 | Nate quotes Opus pricing at $4 input/$20 output per million tokens, twice Sol’s $2/$10, and evaluates output quality against spend rather than price alone.
01:09 | In his Fireflies search over roughly four hours of calls, Sol returns August 17 while Opus identifies September 14 as the latest relevant Q&A; speed did not equal retrieval accuracy.
05:02–10:34 | Nate prefers Opus’s event sizzle reel and Instagram edit for pacing and sound, but says even Opus’s reel would need iteration before publishing.
10:34–18:48 | Sheets/deck and museum-game tests are unscored because the models edited shared files; an edited-in correction places the Sol sheets run at about $3.60 and nine minutes.
18:48 | Opus’s interactive 3D lesson world wins Nate’s subjective comparison, but took about 1h45/$60 versus Sol’s 50 minutes/$8.55.
26:24 | Nate reports Sol winning code repair 100/100 to 97/100 for around $1 and about one-twentieth the Opus cost, after a safety interruption forced a revised prompt.
31:42 | His final count is 7–1 with two invalid tests; he reports $213/8h40 for Opus against $74.46/5h51 for Sol and proposes Opus orchestrating narrow Sol worker tasks.

chapters.title: Intro & Model Pricing
chapters.description: Nate compares the models on the cost of solving the same tasks, not just on whether one token is cheaper than another. He quotes Opus 5.5 at $4 per million input tokens and $20 output, versus $2 and $10 for GPT-6 Sol, and asks which output would be worth a fixed $100 budget before running his examples.

chapters.title: Meeting Transcripts & Knowledge Retrieval
chapters.description: Nate asks both desktop agents to ingest two Fireflies calls totaling roughly four hours and locate his most recent Q&A mentioning a term that transcripts spell inconsistently. Sol starts quickly and works in parallel, but reports August 17; Opus identifies September 14 as the correct date, so Nate values the slower-looking agent’s retrieval accuracy over early progress.

chapters.title: Website Design
chapters.description: Using identical prompts for a coffee-plus-protein product page, Nate prefers Opus’s realistic can imagery, layered parallax and animated scroll narrative to Sol’s flatter page and packaging-style graphics. Both take about 35 minutes, but he awards the design to Opus despite saying its approximately $18.32 run costs about three times Sol’s $5.89.

chapters.title: Event Sizzle Reel
chapters.description: Both agents receive a Frame.io collection of about 100 GB of AIS event footage and a request for a 30-second promotional edit. Nate judges Opus’s sound effects, music, layered shots and faster pacing more effective at selling the next event; he says it finishes roughly five minutes sooner while costing about twice as much, a premium he would pay for this output.

chapters.title: Instagram Reel Editing
chapters.description: Nate plays edits made from the same Instagram footage and prompt and hears an unwanted hum and little music or animation in Sol’s version. Opus adds typing effects and stronger sound design, winning his preference even though it takes about twice as long and costs about four times as much; he still would iterate further before actually posting it.

chapters.title: Sheets, Slides & Dashboards
chapters.description: Opus produces a spreadsheet, deck, dashboard and local landing page, but Nate recognizes that Sol’s apparently similar files may be the very same deliverables. A log review indicates Sol began modifying files after Opus had already worked in the shared repository, so he refuses to declare a winner and later corrects Sol’s cost and runtime to about $3.60 and nine minutes. The case shows that simultaneous agents need isolated workspaces before their outputs can be compared.

chapters.title: Museum Escape Game
chapters.description: Sol’s miniature-museum story initially looks promising but its mouse is not locked to the game frame, making turning and play difficult. Nate then discovers the agents also edited each other’s files on this task, so he explicitly discards the result rather than crediting one model for the observed game; he notes the large time and cost differences only as contaminated observations.

chapters.title: 3D AI Learning World
chapters.description: With separate deliverables this time, Nate explores Opus’s playable lessons about tokens, context windows and skills, noticing small flaws such as balls sticking in a next-word demonstration. Sol’s alternative has crowded overlays and weaker navigation, so Nate prefers Opus’s teaching experience despite roughly $60 and one hour 45 minutes versus $8.55 and 50 minutes for Sol.

chapters.title: Interactive Trip Planning
chapters.description: Nate asks each agent to turn a vague October itinerary into an explorable globe with event, nature and booking links. Sol asks clarifying questions and supplies clickable travel stops, but Opus’s globe is more immersive and includes San Francisco Tech Week and other relevant events that Nate wanted; with similar runtimes and about triple the cost, Opus wins his subjective test.

chapters.title: Code Review & Repair
chapters.description: Nate uses an externally designed codebase challenge to test analysis and repair rather than visual design, and reports Sol at 100/100 versus Opus at 97/100. Sol costs roughly $1 and about one-twentieth as much as Opus, but a cybersecurity refusal pauses its run and requires a modified prompt for both, so this is a useful first-hand result rather than a controlled universal ranking.

chapters.title: Building a Course in Skool
chapters.description: Both agents populate a Skool course from Nate’s supplied lesson videos and descriptions; he finds the uploaded material and supporting links broadly comparable. Opus duplicates some links but makes only the overall course a draft instead of every lesson, and wins this browser task because Nate says it was faster and cheaper despite that small defect.

chapters.title: Drawing in Canva
chapters.description: Asked to redraw a reference image in Canva using drawing tools, Opus produces a likeness Nate likes much more than his past tests. Sol first generates an image instead of drawing it and, after further attempts, delivers drawings Nate considers very poor; he awards the visual browser task to Opus despite roughly 30 extra minutes and fourfold cost.

chapters.title: Results & Final Thoughts
chapters.description: Nate counts seven Opus wins and one Sol win, with the shared-file spreadsheet and museum tests excluded from scoring. He reports total runs of about 8h40/$213 for Opus and 5h51/$74.46 for Sol, while warning through the earlier correction that costs need auditing; his practical preference is Opus for creative judgment and orchestration, with cheaper Sol assigned precise worker or repair tasks.

quick_takeaways: Herk prefers Opus for creative work and judgment, and cheaper Sol for defined worker tasks or code repair. Quoted input/output prices are $4/$20 versus $2/$10 per million tokens.

Opus produced his preferred animated website, event promo, learning world, trip globe and Canva drawing. Higher quality often cost substantially more; neither first-pass Instagram reel was ready to publish.
Check retrieval accuracy as well as speed: Sol returned an older Q&A as the latest, while Opus found the intended September session.
Sol won the reported code-repair test, scoring 100/100 versus 97/100 for around $1 and roughly one-twentieth the spend. A safety interruption and prompt revision complicate the comparison.
Isolate each agent's repository before comparing outputs. Shared files contaminated the dashboard and museum-game tests, so Herk discarded both rather than credit either model.
Final reported totals: seven Opus wins, one Sol win, two discarded tests; roughly $213/8h40 versus $74.46/5h51. Task selection and verification matter more than a single overall winner.

videos.summary:
Chamath Palihapitiya argues that AI will change the mix of work, though his expectation that it creates more jobs than it removes is a forecast, not a measured result. His personal response is to cultivate taste and judgment while using models to gather and organize information. He gives examples of agents he maintains for multi-party negotiations, psychological blind spots, household finances and health, emphasizing that their usefulness depends on continual curation and checking their output.

He advises people to build small tools for their own lives and professions rather than treating AI as infallible. A loan officer, for example, might automate processing yet still make the consequential approval decision. Asked what children should study, he tentatively suggests engineering and physics for an understanding of constraints, and philosophy, politics and economics for incentives and human behavior, while saying he does not know the definitive answer.

He distinguishes demonstrated model capability from uncertain effects on jobs and prosperity. Because social media amplifies fear and misinformation, he argues that AI companies should collectively invest in public infrastructure and credible transition plans, drawing an analogy to libraries and schools funded during industrialization. His conclusion is that people must be able to see a place for themselves in the transition; this is an argument about how to manage change, not evidence that its eventual benefits are guaranteed.
videos.why_valuable: A first-person account of specific AI-assisted decision workflows alongside a candid distinction between current model capabilities and uncertain social outcomes; useful for deciding what to prototype and what human judgment to preserve.
key_takeaways: AI can support decisions, but the speaker treats taste and judgment as enduring human responsibilities.
His personal agents cover negotiations, psychological framing, portfolio spending and health; each requires maintenance and output review.
Start with a practical tool in your own domain and discover its limitations through use.
He says employment and abundance outcomes remain uncertain despite his optimism.
He calls on AI leaders to build trust and transition support rather than relying on optimistic messaging alone.

chapters.title: Work disruption and the role of judgment
chapters.description: Palihapitiya predicts some jobs will disappear and different work will emerge, but frames the total employment gain as his expectation rather than a settled fact. With knowledge easier to retrieve, he says the differentiating skill is choosing how to interpret and apply it; his negotiation agent is introduced as a way to model trade-offs, hidden parties and incentives in high-stakes deals.

chapters.title: Personal agents for decisions and optionality
chapters.description: He layers business and psychology books into a second filter to check for weaknesses in his own negotiation thinking. He then describes an agent that tracks household spending and tests low-risk income scenarios with Monte Carlo simulations so he can avoid debt, plus a health workflow that compares blood tests, eating habits and research rather than offering a one-off answer.

chapters.title: Curation rather than autopilot
chapters.description: A foundation model becomes more useful to him after he has built and repeatedly updated small services for negotiations, finances, health and sometimes parenting. He warns that an uncurated system can recycle fashionable advice such as saunas and cold plunges, so he edits instructions, inspects the answers and decides what fits his own goals instead of outsourcing his judgment.

chapters.title: Building tools at work and learning their limits
chapters.description: For a loan officer, automated paperwork could free time to inspect patterns while the decision to approve a loan remains a human responsibility. He recommends making a tool for a real problem and testing what it cannot do; when asked about education, he offers physics and engineering for understanding constraints and philosophy, politics and economics for studying incentives, explicitly without claiming a definitive curriculum.

chapters.title: What is known and what is amplified
chapters.description: He separates the observation that current models are capable from speculation about job losses or universal abundance, saying both outcomes remain uncertain. Social platforms reward attention, he argues, so inaccurate claims about either future can spread quickly; his industrialization analogy is meant to explain why managing public understanding matters during a disruptive transition.

chapters.title: Collective investment and public trust
chapters.description: He invokes industrial-era libraries and schools as examples of infrastructure that helped people adapt when work moved from farms and small makers to factories. He wants AI-company leaders to pool effort behind similarly credible transition support, because without it people may not trust claims of later benefits while experiencing immediate losses; he closes by arguing that everyone needs a way to participate rather than merely hear reassuring predictions.

quick_takeaways: Use AI to gather and organize information while cultivating your own taste and judgment. Chamath's response to disruption is to become better at choosing, not to assume the model's recommendation is correct.

Build small agents around actual decisions: he uses them for negotiations, psychological blind spots, household finances and health. Keep curating their context and checking output instead of putting consequential decisions on autopilot.
Look for processing work in your profession that can be automated while preserving accountable human decisions. His loan-officer example separates document handling from the final approval.

For education, he tentatively favors engineering/physics for constraints and philosophy/politics/economics for incentives and people. He explicitly does not claim a definitive answer about what children should study.
Separate current model capabilities from forecasts about jobs and prosperity. Fear-amplifying social media is poor evidence for either guaranteed abundance or inevitable mass displacement.

He argues AI companies should invest collectively in public infrastructure and credible transition plans. People need visible ways to participate in the change, not only promises of future productivity.

Jacklyn Dallas interviews Mark Zuckerberg about Meta’s Muse personal AI and how Meta’s long-running AI, glasses, and virtual-presence investments might converge. Zuckerberg says the personal-agent challenge is not just general reasoning or code generation: the system must use memory and tools to carry out goals, keep sensitive facts discreet, and allow users to set its personality. He describes a separate virtual computer for each user, a credential store, security monitoring, and work toward confidential computing; these are Meta’s stated designs and goals, not independent security guarantees.

His 2030 vision blends in-person and holographic participation with an AI able to see and hear context through glasses. He says AI became capable sooner than affordable, ubiquitous holographic displays, so the product path will be iterative. He discusses the Llama 4 setback and reorganizing a smaller research team, then explains how he turns lengthy internal writing into shorter public communications and why building and learning new skills remain personally motivating.

The conversation turns to Biohub’s tool-building approach to biology, including a proposed virtual-cell model; Zuckerberg declines to name a year for curing disease and distinguishes cure, prevention, and management. Finally he discusses large compute clusters alongside potential efficiency breakthroughs, and argues that reliable alignment, discretion, training-time safeguards, and user trust are necessary to make a widely used personal agent. Predictions about superintelligence and 2030 are his projections, not established outcomes.
videos.why_valuable: An extended primary-source account of Meta’s proposed agent architecture, privacy model, glasses roadmap, research restructuring and safety rationale, with concrete examples and explicit uncertainty around predictions.
key_takeaways: Muse aims to act on individual goals while controlling what private context it discloses.
Meta proposes per-user virtual machines, credential isolation and a monitoring agent; confidential-VM protection is described as work in progress.
Zuckerberg says AI arrived before inexpensive ubiquitous holograms and expects product integration to unfold iteratively.
He reorganized model research after Llama 4 missed its trajectory and describes scaling Muse as a current priority.
Biohub aims to build reusable biological tools; his disease timeline and superintelligence claims remain forecasts.

chapters.title: Making Massive Bets
chapters.description: Zuckerberg traces Meta’s AI work from the early News Feed and research lab to a launch he says already has millions of users after roughly two weeks. He describes quickly recognizing an agent experience worth scaling, while the interviewer connects that launch to earlier investments in glasses and virtual worlds; the introductory framing is a company vision rather than proof of future adoption.

chapters.title: What Makes Personal AI Different from General AI?
chapters.description: An assistant that books a restaurant must know a user’s allergy or pregnancy without automatically exposing those facts to a third party, Zuckerberg argues. He says coding skill matters because an agent can write code in the background, but discretion, persistent memory, a recurring check of goals, and a steerable voice-and-avatar interface distinguish his proposed personal product from a coding tool.

chapters.title: Why Meta Gives Every AI Agent Its Own Computer
chapters.description: Rather than storing everyone’s sensitive context in one shared pool, Meta provisions each agent a virtual machine and proposes confidential-computing protections that Zuckerberg says are still being developed. He also describes a credential store that fills in passwords without showing them to the model and a Sentinel agent watching incoming and outgoing data; the argument is that secure architecture must underpin trust, not merely a reassuring interface.

chapters.title: How Do You Shape AI’s Personality?
chapters.description: Zuckerberg rejects the idea of one optimal model persona: the initial setup asks users what temperament they want, and they can change voice, avatar and behavior later. He contrasts an earlier sarcastic assistant with his current more straightforward one, showing why steerability is treated as a product capability rather than a single designer-chosen character.

chapters.title: Mark’s Surprising Prediction About AI and the Metaverse
chapters.description: He expected lifelike holograms to arrive before advanced personal AI, but now says the order has reversed. He recalls a laborious earlier hologram demo and discusses improvements in setup, alongside unresolved questions about how people represent themselves digitally; glasses offer an AI access to the user’s perspective even while mass-market holographic displays remain hard to make affordable.

chapters.title: What 2030 Looks Like
chapters.description: Zuckerberg imagines friends playing poker together with some participants present as holograms and even the cards digitally rendered, rather than everyone joining a flat video call. He says today’s popular glasses often omit displays for cost and size, while display-equipped versions and a planned upgrade from one-turn voice replies to Muse point toward a gradual blending of physical and digital experiences.

chapters.title: Mark’s Founder Mindset
chapters.description: He says Llama 4 fell behind the trajectory Meta needed and concludes that a large, parallelized feed-and-ads-style team was the wrong structure for frontier model research. The resulting Meta Superintelligence Lab combines a smaller, tightly coordinated group with rebuilt infrastructure; when Muse launched well, attention shifted to GPU capacity and product-team integrations rather than treating the earlier setback as irreversible.

chapters.title: How Mark Writes and Shares His Vision
chapters.description: Zuckerberg describes drafting a roughly 15-page internal statement after debates over employment, data centers, government relations, national security and misuse risks. He then compressed it into a one-page public op-ed and a short video, explaining that different audiences need different levels of detail and that writing helps him refine his own thinking before making a shared company position.

chapters.title: What Drives Mark to Build?
chapters.description: Building is an intrinsic creative need for him, but he says learning new skills also requires extended practice rather than a clever shortcut. He recounts struggling with spoken languages before deliberately studying Mandarin, and compares that process to martial arts, flying and music; the point is that a founder’s long-term development depends on repeatedly investing time in unfamiliar domains.

chapters.title: A Golden Age for Builders
chapters.description: He distinguishes a drive to make products from the care-oriented motivation he sees in doctors and nurses, while agreeing that many people want more agency over what they create. He expects agents to lower the cost of turning a vague idea into an initial sketch that a person can refine, though this is an aspiration about broader access to building rather than a measured social outcome.

chapters.title: How Close Are We to Curing All Diseases?
chapters.description: Biohub’s strategy, he says, is to fund shared scientific instruments and platforms rather than attempt to cure every illness itself. He points to a virtual-cell model that could simulate proteins and cellular effects before physical experiments, avoids giving an exact new deadline, and clarifies that success may mean curing, preventing, or managing conditions so they no longer impair life.

chapters.title: The Most Common Thought in Mark’s Head
chapters.description: Immediately after launching Muse, Zuckerberg says the team is collecting reactions, widening access and extracting more capacity from existing GPUs. He also wants to improve the Muse Spark models and push frontier quality, so his near-term focus is a feedback-and-scaling cycle rather than a fixed account of what the product will ultimately become.

chapters.title: What Breakthroughs Come Next?
chapters.description: He describes a gigawatt-scale Ohio training cluster and a planned five-gigawatt Louisiana facility as a way to push existing methods further, while admitting research may reveal better architectures. Comparing power-hungry clusters with the much more efficient human brain, he argues that infrastructure scaling and algorithmic efficiency should both be pursued; his AGI expectations remain speculative.

chapters.title: How to Win AI Safety
chapters.description: He says an assistant cannot earn mass trust if it technically completes a task while betraying the user’s intent or values. In addition to user feedback, he emphasizes training-time alignment, resistance to reward hacking, discretion and hardening the agent’s virtual computer; he argues that the incentive to keep users should motivate labs, while acknowledging those safeguards took extra development time.

quick_takeaways: A personal agent needs persistent goals, memory, tools and discretion, not only strong chat or code generation. Zuckerberg also emphasizes letting users shape its personality.

Meta describes a separate virtual computer per user, a credential store and security monitoring. Confidential computing is a development goal; these descriptions are not independent guarantees of privacy.

Glasses could supply visual and audio context while holographic participation blends remote and in-person presence. Zuckerberg's 2030 picture is a direction for iterative products, not a committed shipping schedule.
He describes recovering from Llama 4 setbacks by reorganizing research into a smaller team. His own communication workflow turns lengthy internal writing into shorter public explanations.
Biohub focuses on tools for biology, including a proposed virtual-cell model. Cure, prevention and disease management are distinct goals; he declines to promise a year when all disease will be cured.

Large compute investment and efficiency breakthroughs can both matter. Broad personal-agent adoption still depends on trustworthy alignment, training safeguards and appropriate handling of sensitive information.

videos.title: Rails World 2026 Opening Keynote - DHH
videos.description:
DHH opens Rails World 2026 in Austin with a keynote on the age of AI agents: why 37signals has gone "pencils down" on handwritten code, why Rails' convention over configuration is built for this moment, and why the only play left is total optimism.

Thank you, Shopify, for sponsoring the editing and post-production of these videos. Check out insights from the Engineering team at: https://shopify.engineering/

#rails #rubyonrails #railsworld #tech 

[00:00:00] — Welcome to Rails World 2026: DHH on AI euphoria
[00:01:50] — What portrait painters can teach us about AI
[00:11:20] — November 24, 2025: the Kodak Brownie of our era
[00:12:43] — The trough of disillusionment, and the leap that followed
[00:16:02] — From the 10x programmer to the 1,000x programmer
[00:18:13] — "Look at all the things I'm not doing": the Rails moment
[00:20:45] — 37signals goes pencils down on hand-written code
[00:22:12] — What vibe-coding Basecamp 5 taught us
[00:24:04] — Rebuilding HEY as native apps
[00:28:14] — Rethinking HEY's backend with agents
[00:33:04] — Where does this leave Ruby and Rails?
[00:34:23] — Agent evals with Evil Martians and the Rails Foundation
[00:36:28] — 150,000 lines of code in a month
[00:38:06] — English: the programming language DHH likes better than Ruby
[00:39:21] — Retiring from hand-written code, with joy
[00:42:49] — Rethinking software architecture for the age of agents
[00:45:23] — Bring your own agent: why every app needs a CLI
[00:48:05] — Omarchy: fixing the whole computer
[00:51:21] — One-shot apps: a calculator, a writing app, a video editor, and Hype

[00:58:26] — P(bloom) over P(doom)
[01:00:49] — The case for total optimism
videos.summary:
At Rails World 2026, David Heinemeier Hansson argues that agentic coding has changed software production as sharply as cheap photography changed portraiture. He dates his own inflection point to Claude Opus 4.5 and describes a subsequent short-lived dip in confidence before more capable models persuaded him that developers can assign outcomes to agents. His 100x–1,000x productivity comparisons are rhetorical estimates, not benchmark results.

He says 37signals has made handwritten code the exception and is exploring six native HEY clients and a Rust backend, even though Basecamp 5 exposed architectural problems when many designer-written agent PRs were combined. A back-of-the-envelope estimate claims the new HEY backend could consume far less CPU and memory, but it is not presented as a measured production result. He still sees a role for Rails on install-free web applications, citing its conventions and token-efficient structure, and describes Rails agent evaluations built with Evil Martians.

DHH advocates handing tasks to agents asynchronously, exposing CLIs so a user’s own agent can work across apps, and revisiting old assumptions about code abstraction. He demonstrates small agent-built Omarchy apps and his Markdown-based presentation tool Hype, then argues that reduced development cost can enable software optimization. He acknowledges security risks but rejects confident forecasts of mass job loss or catastrophe, ending with a forceful call for optimistic experimentation. This is his perspective, not independent validation of his forecasts or performance claims.
videos.why_valuable: A first-hand statement of 37signals’ agent-led engineering policy with concrete HEY, Basecamp, Rails-eval, CLI and Omarchy examples, plus clearly identifiable claims that require independent measurement.
key_takeaways: 37signals says it now treats handwritten code as an exception and fixes the agent workflow when it fails.
Basecamp 5 showed that individually acceptable agent PRs can damage architecture in aggregate.
HEY native clients and a proposed Rust backend are exploratory; dramatic efficiency numbers are back-of-the-envelope estimates.
Rails conventions may reduce agent work for web services that should not require an install.
DHH recommends app CLIs for users’ own agents and argues for security work without pretending to predict all social outcomes.

chapters.title: Welcome to Rails World 2026: DHH on AI euphoria
chapters.description: DHH welcomes the Rails community in Austin and calls his enthusiasm for agents “AI euphoria,” while conceding the speed of change can feel unsettling. He says the endpoint is hard to forecast because predictions become obsolete quickly, setting up a talk that argues for experimentation despite uncertainty.

chapters.title: What portrait painters can teach us about AI
chapters.description: He traces portrait-making from costly commissioned paintings to Kodak’s inexpensive Brownie and finally to phone photos taken almost without friction. The new camera reduced the economic value of literal portrait painting but helped push artists toward other forms; he uses that shift and the huge rise in everyday photos to argue that automation can transform work while expanding what gets created.

chapters.title: November 24, 2025: the Kodak Brownie of our era
chapters.description: He identifies the release of Opus 4.5 in an affordable coding-agent harness as the moment the technology became useful to him for making software. He says subsequent experiments and open-weight alternatives spread access quickly, comparing this expanding ecosystem to the many cameras and practices that followed the first mass-market models.

chapters.title: The trough of disillusionment, and the leap that followed
chapters.description: After enjoying fast Kimi K2.5, he says model releases from February through May felt disappointing and briefly fed a narrative that progress had stalled. He says a later Opus release changed his experience from requesting small coding tasks to assigning a problem and receiving a mergeable result; he also welcomes later OpenAI and DeepSeek releases as signs of competition, while these are his subjective impressions.

chapters.title: From the 10x programmer to the 1,000x programmer
chapters.description: He revisits an older study behind the disputed idea that one programmer can outperform another by an order of magnitude. He then speculates that the gap between someone without agents and someone adept at using them could reach hundreds or a thousand times, explicitly saying exact acceleration is unknown; the numbers express his view of a changed competitive landscape, not a controlled comparison.

chapters.title: "Look at all the things I'm not doing": the Rails moment
chapters.description: A clip from his 2005 Rails presentation shows routes and templates working without repetitive configuration, which he compares to present-day work delegated to agents. He says he has produced much more software while personally writing little code for months, framing reduced mechanical effort as a continuation of Rails’ original productivity argument.

chapters.title: 37signals goes pencils down on hand-written code
chapters.description: At 37signals, manually writing code is now treated as an exceptional condition rather than the normal development path, he says. If an agent cannot produce a desired change, the team might intervene temporarily, but should repair its workflow or tooling rather than normalize repeated human patching; his informal show of hands suggests many attendees already write little code weekly.

chapters.title: What vibe-coding Basecamp 5 taught us
chapters.description: Designers produced roughly 20–30 plausible individual PRs for Basecamp 5, but their combined changes damaged the application’s architecture, so the team returned to manual review for that release. DHH now calls that retreat premature and says the better question is how to improve coordination and review with stronger agents, distinguishing the shipped hybrid approach from his newer policy.

chapters.title: Rebuilding HEY as native apps
chapters.description: DHH says 37signals is developing a new HEY using multiple native clients instead of relying on a web-app compromise originally chosen for small-team productivity. He shows an early Windows output that needed another prompt before it was closer to acceptable, and cites Shopify’s native Shop rewrite as another example; he presents cheap generation of native interfaces as a reason to reconsider earlier cross-platform trade-offs.

chapters.title: Rethinking HEY's backend with agents
chapters.description: He proposes using agents to rewrite HEY’s backend in Rust, a language whose code he says he dislikes reading but whose compiled performance he wants. His estimates of 99% less CPU, 95% less memory and possible single-Pi peak capacity are explicitly back-of-the-envelope; he also describes experimenting with asynchronous, coworker-like agent assignments inside Basecamp instead of watching a chat stream.

chapters.title: Where does this leave Ruby and Rails?
chapters.description: He distinguishes a native email client with a Rust server from services where users need immediate web access without installing anything. For those services, he argues Rails’ conventional names and structure can lower the amount of instruction an agent needs and preserve the framework’s usefulness, rather than implying every 37signals project should migrate away from Ruby.

chapters.title: Agent evals with Evil Martians and the Rails Foundation
chapters.description: Evil Martians, working for the Rails Foundation, had to toughen Rails agent evaluations after agents reached roughly 95% completion on the first tests, he says. He advocates evaluating actual feature work and asking high-level outcome questions instead of dictating implementation, using his limited Rust knowledge as an example of judging generated software from the outside.

chapters.title: 150,000 lines of code in a month
chapters.description: DHH contrasts his prior average of about 30,000 lines of production Ruby per year with his claim of 150,000 generated lines in one August. He cautions that verbose Rust and line-count differences make this an imperfect productivity metric; the example chiefly illustrates how drastically his own workflow and the mix of languages have changed.

chapters.title: English: the programming language DHH likes better than Ruby
chapters.description: He now enjoys specifying desired outcomes in English even more than writing Ruby, despite natural language being less precise and deterministic. He recalls beginning programming because he wanted things built, then falling in love with coding itself; agent collaboration, for him, returns attention to results without denying the value he found in the older craft.

chapters.title: Retiring from hand-written code, with joy
chapters.description: He says he has effectively stopped being a professional programmer who writes code by hand, but looks back fondly on decades of that work. He predicts the economics will push most developers toward directing agents and making things instead, comparing the transition to earlier computing milestones; this is a personal forecast, not evidence that every team has already changed.

chapters.title: Rethinking software architecture for the age of agents
chapters.description: If many agents can modify a codebase in parallel, he questions whether centralized abstractions remain as useful when they become shared choke points. He says cheap repetition and synchronization change architectural trade-offs but admits nobody has a settled blueprint, inviting developers to rethink methodology, cycle lengths and responsibility for specifications rather than prescribing a universal pattern.

chapters.title: Bring your own agent: why every app needs a CLI
chapters.description: He rejects embedding a separate chatbot concierge in every app when users could connect their own assistant to many services. Using HEY’s CLI, he says an agent recovered a years-old email from fragmentary memories about sneakers and a podcast where ordinary Elasticsearch search struggled; that concrete example supports his call for applications to expose practical command-line interfaces.

chapters.title: Omarchy: fixing the whole computer
chapters.description: Omarchy is his example of applying the same agent-assisted repair mindset to an entire computer rather than just a single app. He cites approximately $20 million raised and progress from a multi-minute installation to demos taking tens of seconds or less, presenting installation speed as an expression of iterative ambition rather than a benchmark for every machine.

chapters.title: One-shot apps: a calculator, a writing app, a video editor, and Hype
chapters.description: He describes making an Omarchy-themed calculator from a screenshot prompt, then a writing app, a video editor, and Hype presentation software without inspecting all the generated C++ himself. The calculator reached a repository and installation image quickly, while Hype uses Markdown and produces a small executable; these examples illustrate his emphasis on rapid iteration, not proof that all one-shot outputs ship untouched.

chapters.title: The performance payoff: half a megabyte
chapters.description: He argues that expensive programmer hours once encouraged teams to tolerate bloated software, mentioning a large desktop music client as a contrast. With agents able to try overnight optimization passes, he expects small binaries and faster apps to become easier to justify; the half-megabyte Hype binary is his demonstration, not a universal performance guarantee.

chapters.title: AI concerns, security, and why predictions fail
chapters.description: He acknowledges that agent security needs active preparation while questioning confident predictions of economic collapse from automation. Drawing on the history of ATMs, bank branches and even nuclear technology, he argues past experts often missed second-order effects; these analogies explain his skepticism about forecasts but do not settle the actual risks of AI.

chapters.title: P(bloom) over P(doom)
chapters.description: Rather than assume negative outcomes are inevitable, he advocates addressing concrete failures, citing a Rails image-library vulnerability and a proposed HotCell isolation effort. He pairs that engineering response with his account of teller employment after ATMs and nuclear-energy debates to claim people can correct course; the probabilities he assigns to flourishing over catastrophe are opinion, not quantified evidence.

chapters.title: The case for total optimism
chapters.description: He closes by urging programmers to treat accessible agents as an expansion of who can make software, not only as new competition. A children’s Omarchy variant serves as his example of younger users embracing change without old habits to unlearn, and he asks the audience to work through uncertainty with deliberate optimism rather than withdraw.

quick_takeaways: Assign outcomes to agents asynchronously instead of treating them only as coding assistants. DHH says 37signals now makes handwritten code the exception; his enormous productivity multipliers are rhetorical, not measured benchmarks.

Cheap generation does not remove architecture work: combining many designer-created agent PRs exposed problems in Basecamp 5. Review how changes fit together, not only whether each feature works alone.

Lower development cost makes previously expensive native clients, backend rewrites and optimization worth reconsidering. The proposed HEY Rust backend's CPU/memory savings are estimates, not production measurements.

Rails still suits install-free web applications through conventions and compact structure. DHH describes agent evaluations with Evil Martians rather than assuming a new model invalidates the framework.
Expose CLIs so users can bring their own agents across applications. His small Omarchy apps and Markdown presentation tool show opportunities for personal software and simpler workflows.

Revisit old assumptions about abstraction and development economics, while checking security and the actual result. His optimistic jobs and catastrophe forecasts are perspectives, not established outcomes.
