The WorldofAI host presents Claude Opus 5.5 as a major Opus 5 upgrade for coding, computer use and knowledge work, quoting Anthropic's roughly Fable 5.1-level performance, around 30% faster execution and 40% lower per-task cost than Opus 5. He cites external prelaunch evaluation and Anthropic's alignment claims, as well as its reported benchmark wins, a 680,000-line migration in under a day and 39 of 40 web pages optimized without breaking behavior; these are reported claims rather than tasks he independently reproduces here. His own WoAI Bench ranks it above GPT-6 Astra, but he also promotes that benchmark. He reports a 20% higher Claude Code five-hour session limit and roughly 25% more usage, and quotes base API pricing of $4 per million input and $20 per million output tokens, versus $8/$40 for the faster mode (up to 2.5× speed). Despite repeating cheaper-per-task claims, he warns it can consume many tokens.

After explaining Claude, API and his own harness access, he shows community or third-party one-shot examples: a more polished Mario Kart-style game than a Fable 5.1 version given the same prompt, a launch-video lookalike and a 13,000-tile animated mosaic coded without external image assets. A side-by-side Three.js autonomous-car scene looks more detailed to him with Opus than GPT-6 Astra; a Nintendo Switch SVG looks good but reportedly uses about 20–27% of a $20 subscription's session allowance at max reasoning. These are visual demonstrations and comparisons, not blinded standardized tests; he suggests using a cheaper model for lighter work and only speculates about a future Haiku 5.5.

In a Minecraft-like game he can change settings, create a world, see mobs, blocks and an inventory, but the sound is unexpectedly loud and his assessment of cave systems reverses after he tries to find one; he also says its lighting is weaker than a Fable example. A separately generated Three.js Call of Duty Zombies-style demo has atmospheric lighting, purchasable items, doors and a rebuildable barrier, which he finds unusually polished. These walkthroughs establish visible features, not that either clone is complete or robust under broad testing.

He calls Opus 5.5 his frontend favorite and shows an Opus 5-versus-5.5 volcano-island scene with a more elaborate cutaway, creatures and environment in the newer result. Crucially, this particular generation costs about $3.40 with 5.5 versus $1.60 with Opus 5, despite the lower token-list price and his general cheaper-per-task framing: richer output can cost more on a specific prompt. He finishes by calling it the best available model in his assessment, but recommends trying it on complex tasks rather than spending it on everything; the closing minutes are promotions, not additional test results.
videos.why_valuable: A visual coding buyer can inspect concrete games, animations, Three.js scenes and an SVG alongside published prices and the host’s practical session-limit caveat. The decision is to trial Opus 5.5 on demanding frontend or creative-coding work, then measure actual tokens, session usage and output quality against cheaper alternatives; several impressive examples are third-party showcases, and the shown $3.40 versus $1.60 run complicates the broad efficiency claim.
key_takeaways: The host reports Anthropic’s roughly Fable 5.1-class performance, ~30% faster and ~40% cheaper per task than Opus 5; benchmark and large-code-migration figures are cited claims, not independently recreated in this video.
Quoted base pricing is $4 input/$20 output per million tokens, with a fast option at $8/$40 and up to 2.5× speed; token-heavy max-reasoning jobs can still exhaust a subscription quickly.
The Nintendo Switch SVG reportedly uses about 20–27% of a $20-plan session allowance, making model/effort selection important for day-to-day work.

Community demos include a Mario Kart-style game, a coded launch-video replica and a 13,000-tile animation; a Three.js car comparison looks better to the host than Astra, but these are not blinded benchmarks.

The Minecraft-style clone includes editable world settings, mobs and inventory, yet the host cannot confirm caves and judges its lighting worse than a Fable example; the zombies demo shows doors, purchases and barrier rebuilding.
An Opus 5.5 volcano-island scene is richer than its Opus 5 counterpart but costs about $3.40 versus $1.60 on that shown generation, so lower rates do not guarantee lower cost for every request.
His final recommendation is to reserve Opus 5.5 for complex output and route simple tasks to cheaper models, despite calling it his current overall and frontend favorite.

chapters.title: Intro
chapters.description: The presenter introduces Opus 5.5 as a substantial improvement in agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work, claiming performance near Fable 5.1 at a lower cost than Opus 5. He then places the launch in the context of AI labs discussing slower frontier releases and says external evaluators reviewed it before launch. Anthropic's reported alignment evaluation, described as its most comprehensive yet, provides another part of his opening case for the model.

chapters.title: Better Than Fable 5.1
chapters.description: The presenter reiterates that Opus 5.5 performs at roughly Fable 5.1's level on most tasks, but distinguishes its operating economics from the older Opus 5. He claims it runs about 30% faster and costs about 40% less per task, then uses those savings to lead into an announced improvement for Claude Code users.

chapters.title: Rate Limit Reset
chapters.description: Claude Code's five-hour session allowance is said to rise by 20%, while the cheaper model should let users accomplish roughly 25% more work within the limit. The presenter also describes an on-demand reset for eligible paid users, framing it as more flexibility when a session runs short. He briefly interrupts the explanation to ask viewers to subscribe before moving toward his benchmark results.

chapters.title: WOAI Bench
chapters.description: The presenter says his World of AI benchmark and vibe-coding platform tested the model across multiple domains and ranked it above Astra overall. He singles out agentic reasoning and debugging as strengths, while asserting that other evaluated areas also set new standards. He closes by inviting viewers to test their own model endpoints on the platform, including its free starting option.

chapters.title: Benchmarks
chapters.description: The presenter reviews reported gains over Opus 5 and rival frontier models in coding-oriented tests including Terminal Bench, Cursor Bench, and GDP Evolve, then points to strong OSWorld computer-use results. He cites Anthropic's account of a tester completing a 680,000-line code migration in under a day and describes a web-page optimization result covering 39 of 40 pages without breaking behavior. A single-prompt polished-game example broadens his case beyond coding benchmarks, before he turns to Artificial Analysis's index ranking.

chapters.title: Best Model Ever
chapters.description: The presenter completes his point about Artificial Analysis by saying Opus 5.5 holds the top position on its index. He pairs that ranking with a claimed 20% price reduction and a larger cache-hit discount, shifting the emphasis from raw leaderboard performance to the cost of using the model. This brief transition sets up his more detailed efficiency and pricing breakdown.

chapters.title: Pricing
chapters.description: The presenter says lower per-token prices and fewer tokens per task amount to roughly 40% less token cost than Opus 5, and describes a fast mode offering up to 2.5 times the speed. He lists base pricing at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, versus $8 and $40 respectively for fast mode. He then cautions that the model can consume many tokens in practice, complicating the efficiency claim, before briefly promoting his newsletter and transitioning to access options.

chapters.title: How To Use
chapters.description: For direct access, the presenter points viewers to the Claude chatbot and Anthropic's API platform. He also offers his own benchmark and vibe-coding harness as a way to run evaluations and experiment with the model rather than relying only on his demos. The segment ends by directing viewers to the linked resources for getting started.

chapters.title: Mario Kart Demo
chapters.description: A third-party one-shot game generation produces a playable kart-racing scene with recognizable Mario and Luigi characters. The presenter points out speed boosts and collectible perks as evidence that the result includes game mechanics, not just attractive visuals. Comparing it with Fable 5.1 given the same prompt, he says the earlier model failed to deliver comparable quality and calls this one of his strongest coding examples.

chapters.title: Video Creation
chapters.description: The presenter shows a coded recreation of the model's launch video, saying its creator supplied the original post but prohibited external music, sound, and image assets. He treats the resulting animation as evidence that the model can build moving visual content from code rather than simply embed media. A second example, an animated mosaic of around 13,000 individually drawn tiles with no images, extends his argument about creative coding beyond conventional web development.

chapters.title: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 Astra
chapters.description: Both models are given the same request to construct a three-dimensional autonomous vehicle, giving the presenter a side-by-side visual comparison. He favors the Opus result for its vehicle proportions, physics, shaders, and carefully modeled camera and sensor details. The comparison ends with his claim that these components make its rendition more faithful to the real car than Astra's version.

chapters.title: SVG Demo
chapters.description: The presenter displays an SVG rendition of a Nintendo Switch generated with the model's maximum reasoning setting, clarifying that it is an AI-produced graphic rather than official Nintendo media. He says this single generation consumed about 20–27% of a $20 plan's session allowance, making the impressive result expensive in practical usage terms. He recommends reserving the highest reasoning setting for difficult projects and moving routine work to a lighter model.

chapters.title: Haiku 5.5
chapters.description: Correcting his previous suggestion to use Haiku for simpler tasks, the presenter says he meant Sonnet as the currently available alternative. He adds that Anthropic is trying to bring Haiku back and speculates that a 5.5 version might arrive in the coming weeks. This short aside closes the discussion of cheaper task routing before the next generated-game showcase begins.

chapters.title: Minecraft Clone
chapters.description: The presenter explores a generated sandbox game whose controls allow adjustments to sound, clouds, brightness, and field of view before creating a new world. He praises the textured environment and demonstrates sounds tied to breaking blocks and interacting with different animal mobs, including sheep and cows. The game also includes familiar sandbox functions and an inventory in which gathered blocks can be turned into crafted items.

chapters.title: lol
chapters.description: The attempted crafting demonstration is interrupted when a server from another Claude Code game project launches unexpectedly and plays very loud sounds through the presenter's earbuds. Returning to the sandbox in creative mode, he inspects textured items, a pickaxe, ores, and underground terrain. He finds the lighting weaker than a prior Fable result and cannot confirm the cave systems he expected, but still considers the generated sandbox convincing overall.

chapters.title: Call of Duty Clone
chapters.description: The presenter plays a generated three-dimensional zombies game and emphasizes its lighting, textures, animations, working doors, and purchasable items. During an extended gameplay demonstration, he encounters an instant-kill pickup, rebuilds a barrier with its own animation, fights enemies, and opens another area of the map. He praises the courtyard and connected spaces as well as the overall fidelity, arguing that earlier models could implement some of these mechanics but not at this visual quality.

chapters.title: Frontend Demo
chapters.description: After the game showcase, the presenter broadens his assessment to frontend development and argues that the model now leads that category. He says the quality of the generated output depends on the detail supplied in the request and acknowledges that achieving such results is expensive. His short introduction leads directly into a concrete visual comparison with the previous Opus generation.

chapters.title: Opus 5 vs Opus 5.5
chapters.description: A volcano-island scene with dinosaurs costs about $1.60 on Opus 5 versus about $3.40 on Opus 5.5, making this example more expensive despite the broader pricing claims. The presenter considers the newer result substantially richer, highlighting a cutaway water scene, moving whale, underwater life, vegetation, mammoths, and northern lights. He says this level of detail recurs across his generations and often surpasses Astra, then briefly invites channel support before his conclusion.

chapters.title: Two Cents
chapters.description: The presenter concludes that the improvement is not merely finer visual detail but stronger generation across several domains, despite substantial token consumption. He calls it a leading model with attractive pricing and encourages hands-on testing, while recommending cheaper models for basic tasks and reserving this one for complex work. The closing minutes direct viewers to his benchmark, community, newsletter, and other channels before a final sign-off.

quick_takeaways: The host favors Opus 5.5 for complex frontend and interactive work, with demonstrations of games, SVGs, animations and richer Three.js scenes. Some examples are community supplied rather than first-hand controlled tests.
Quoted base API prices are $4/M input and $20/M output; faster mode is $8/$40. Use a cheaper model for lighter work rather than spending the highest-capability option on every request.
Measure the completed task bill. His newer volcano scene cost about $3.40 versus Opus 5's $1.60, despite lower token rates, because the richer result used more work.
Max reasoning can burn subscription allowance: the Nintendo Switch SVG reportedly consumed about 20–27% of a $20 plan's session allowance. Increased usage limits do not make generation unlimited.
Play through generated games. The Minecraft-style build had loud sound and uncertain cave behavior; visually polished demos do not prove complete mechanics or robust behavior.

The release's speed, migration and benchmark wins are reported claims. Test a real complex task yourself and distinguish demonstrated features from marketing, missing functionality and speculative future models.

videos.summary:
At Dreamforce, Alex Heath asks Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff about his keynote memes, AI hype and San Francisco's recovery. Benioff credits Cisco's John Chambers for his audience-walking style, calls AI still at the “beginning of the beginning,” and contrasts San Francisco's autonomous cars with seeing none during two months in Europe to argue adoption is uneven. He sees the city's AI boom as another reinvention, not its first gold rush. Turning to potential OpenAI and Anthropic IPO wealth, he advocates Salesforce's 1-1-1 pledge of equity, profit and employee time, citing a billion dollars in grants, 11 million volunteer hours, free services for 65,000 nonprofits and schools support; he rejects a choice between good products and philanthropy and says roughly 20,000 companies have adopted the pledge model. These are his account and expectations, not audited results or announced IPOs.

On AI risk, Benioff says CEOs should build responsibility into company culture before belated regulation repeats social media's harms. Discussing a reported OpenAI-model intrusion at Hugging Face, he says its small team and important open-source role prompted him to urge its CEO to seek greater organizational scale, potentially through Salesforce or another buyer; he explicitly cautions against overstating his own role. On enterprise agents, his proposed stack is trustworthy data, applications and analytics/APIs, an agent layer and new interfaces. He attributes Salesforce's Anthropic partnership partly to being unable to invest in OpenAI because of Microsoft's relationship, then says Salesforce also backed other model makers and predicts large Anthropic investment gains. Future acquisitions, he says, remain focused on customer-facing capabilities.

Heath presses him on the “SaaSpocalypse.” Benioff rejects a blanket collapse narrative, citing Salesforce's strong recent quarter, low attrition and long contracts, while acknowledging that technology gets cheaper and firms do fail; he says to test market stories against customers' actual needs rather than social-media or stock narratives. He says Salesforce bought Slack at a high multiple because it envisioned a business-agent platform, and pitches Slack Code, CRM and Slackforce as agent-connected working surfaces; his claims about major customers and future agent use are vendor perspective. For AI pricing he rejects one winner: seats, named agents, usage, consumption such as tokens/storage, completed transactions and shares of customer business outcomes may all suit different buyers. He identifies Slack as a current growth driver and praises the recently acquired Finn for customer-service agents.

Benioff argues “headless Salesforce” is an extension of its older XML, SOAP and REST APIs, not an entirely new invention of MCP: stored metadata about fields, permissions and layouts can be rendered into Slack, Lightning or outside AI interfaces. He expects agents to expose value in enterprise data that humans cannot easily sift. Asked about TIME, which he owns, he asserts that more agents than humans now read its content daily and says it has adapted journalism and advertising for agent access; these readership and advertising-economics claims are his assertions, not independently substantiated in the conversation.

His closing forecast shifts attention from familiar model and infrastructure debates to conversational, adaptive, dynamic interfaces across enterprise software and consumer devices. He imagines an assistant that changes the screen in response to the interview, related reporting and incoming work instead of leaving static icons and inbox lists unchanged. He frames this as bringing deterministic application systems together with probabilistic AI while grounding outputs in data; it is a directional vision rather than a shipped universal interface. The interview ends with thanks and sponsor messages.
videos.why_valuable: Useful for enterprise software strategy: a CEO lays out a concrete thesis connecting data access, Slack distribution, multiple AI pricing units and adaptive interfaces, while Heath challenges him on SaaS displacement, regulation and philanthropy. Treat the Salesforce performance, prospective investment returns, TIME agent readership and product-roadmap claims as an interested executive’s perspective; the actionable decision is where to place customer-data and interface bets, not to take the “SaaSpocalypse is over” slogan as settled fact.
key_takeaways: Benioff sees AI adoption as early and geographically uneven; his San Francisco-versus-Europe autonomous-car contrast is an illustration, not an AI adoption measurement.
His 1-1-1 philanthropy argument combines products and community impact; he cites a billion dollars of grants, 11 million volunteer hours and 65,000 nonprofits served for free as Salesforce figures.

He says the Hugging Face security episode made the limits of a roughly 200-person steward of open-source infrastructure salient and prompted advice about joining a larger organization; he does not claim sole credit for any deal.

Against the SaaSpocalypse thesis he cites Salesforce retention and contract length but concedes cheaper technology and company churn are real; his test is direct customer demand rather than viral market narratives.

Slack is pitched as an agentic enterprise operating surface with communications, application functions and integrations, not simply a chat client; the strategy is an executive’s case for a Salesforce asset.
He proposes six pricing dimensions—named users, named agents, usage, consumption, transaction outcomes and business outcomes—instead of claiming seat pricing has been universally replaced.
His “headless” thesis builds on Salesforce metadata and long-standing APIs, allowing applications to surface in Slack, Lightning and AI clients through newer interfaces such as MCP.

Benioff asserts agent readers now outnumber human readers of TIME and predicts adaptive conversational interfaces will replace static screens; both are claims/forecasts, not independently verified here.

chapters.title: Dreamforce Memes and the AI Hype Cycle
chapters.description: Benioff laughs about becoming a different social-media meme each year, then traces his walk-through-the-audience keynote style to Cisco's John Chambers and explains why Salesforce stages its talks in the round. Turning to AI, he rejects the idea that his comments about Nvidia signal anxiety: the transformation is still at an early stage, and his contrast between San Francisco's autonomous cars and their absence on a recent European trip illustrates how unevenly it is unfolding.

chapters.title: San Francisco’s AI Comeback
chapters.description: Asked whether the city's resurgence can last, Benioff describes San Francisco as a recurring center of reinvention rather than a place enjoying its first technology gold rush. He connects today's OpenAI and Anthropic boom to the city's earlier gold rush, counterculture and commercial history, arguing that the pessimism of a few years ago missed this enduring cycle; the interval then breaks for sponsor messages.

chapters.title: Why AI Leaders Should Give Back
chapters.description: With enormous wealth potentially coming from AI-company IPOs, Benioff explains Salesforce's pledge of one percent of equity, profits and employee time, citing grants, volunteer hours, free nonprofit services and direct support for local schools. When Alex Heath contrasts this with Sam Altman's emphasis on making useful products, Benioff says philanthropy and products are not competing choices: CEOs can use their employees, relationships and corporate culture to deliver community impact while building a business. He points to thousands of companies adopting the pledge model and argues that giving also establishes values and expectations for employees.

chapters.title: AI Safety, Regulation and CEO Responsibility
chapters.description: Benioff argues that responsible leadership must be embedded in a company's culture before policymakers are forced to respond, using the long-delayed reckoning with social media's harms as a warning. The discussion shifts from abstract regulation to the reported OpenAI-model intrusion at Hugging Face: he says its limited security capacity exposed the risks of a small company stewarding important open-source infrastructure. He recounts advising its CEO that joining a larger organization, whether Salesforce or another buyer, could provide the scale needed to protect that role.

chapters.title: Betting on AI Agents and Anthropic
chapters.description: Benioff attributes his early focus on agents partly to San Francisco's technology network and time spent reflecting, but stresses that useful agents require trustworthy data, applications, analytics and adaptable interfaces beneath them. He describes Claude-powered experiences across Salesforce and Slack, then says Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI prevented a Salesforce investment there and pushed the company toward Anthropic and other model makers instead. He expects substantial returns from those bets while keeping future acquisitions focused on products tied to customer relationships and operations.

chapters.title: Is the SaaS Apocalypse Overblown?
chapters.description: Benioff pushes back on predictions that AI will destroy established software vendors, pointing to Salesforce's recent revenue, margins, cash flow, retention and long customer contracts rather than viral market narratives. He says time spent with customers in Europe helped him separate actual purchasing needs from social-media claims that may be intended to move stocks or promote investments. He acknowledges that technology continually gets cheaper and companies can fail, but warns against confidently mapping every winner and loser; much of the remainder of this interval consists of sponsor reads.

chapters.title: Slack as the Operating System for AI Agents
chapters.description: Benioff says Salesforce paid a controversial premium for Slack because it saw the platform as a future business agent, a thesis he credits in part to chief futurist Peter Schwartz. He describes subsequent additions for coding in channels, CRM work and dynamically assembled AI-powered interfaces, alongside adoption by companies such as Meta, Nike and General Motors. Looking ahead, he positions Slack as more than a chat window: its conversations, agent integrations and customizable surfaces can connect people and automated workers across an enterprise, even though core corporate data may live elsewhere.

chapters.title: How Do You Price AI?
chapters.description: Benioff rejects the idea that outcome-based contracts can replace every software seat, laying out a mix of named users, named agents, usage, consumption, completed transactions and measurable business results. Because Salesforce sells many products to customers with different needs, he says it must negotiate across these models rather than impose a single formula. Asked where growth might come from, he singles out Slack's momentum and describes the newly acquired Finn as a fast route for larger as well as smaller companies to deploy customer-facing agents.

chapters.title: Headless Salesforce and Unlocking Business Data
chapters.description: Benioff argues that Salesforce's longstanding APIs and metadata-driven applications already separated business logic from any one screen; newer interfaces such as Claude, Slack and Lightning simply render that underlying structure in different ways. Fields, page layouts, permissions and sharing rules make it possible for AI to surface value buried in customer data while retaining the application context needed to use it. He says Salesforce leaders are already operating through these new surfaces, and illustrates Slack's practical reach with a request he sent to Madrid employees to help a hospitalized colleague's family.

chapters.title: How AI Is Changing TIME and the Media
chapters.description: Benioff defends TIME's emphasis on verifiable reporting despite claims that traditional media is finished, and says automated agents now access its material more often than human readers. Serving those agents has required reworking both articles and advertising so machine-mediated answers and measurable ad readership can support a viable business model. He credits stronger technology, economics, journalism and contributions from outside experts for the publication's progress, while saying he has no ambition to own another media company.

chapters.title: The Future of AI Interfaces
chapters.description: Benioff predicts the most underappreciated AI shift is away from fixed icons and static enterprise screens toward conversational interfaces that adapt continuously to a person's tasks and context. He imagines a device that can suggest better interview questions, incorporate earlier conversations and keep track of messages rather than merely display the same app grid, creating openings for incumbent device makers and new entrants. To make those experiences reliable, he says evolving data, application and agent layers must combine the predictability of conventional software with AI's probabilistic reasoning; the interview closes before brief sponsor messages.

quick_takeaways: Build enterprise agents on trusted data, existing applications and analytics/APIs, then add the agent layer and interface. Benioff's stack grounds probabilistic outputs in deterministic business systems.
Choose pricing around buyer value: seats, named agents, usage/tokens, storage, completed transactions or a share of business outcomes can all work. He rejects one universal AI pricing model.

Test 'SaaSpocalypse' claims against real retention, contracts and customer needs. Cheaper technology can pressure vendors without proving all enterprise software disappears; Salesforce's claims are its CEO's perspective.
Slack is pitched as an agent working surface with code and CRM access. Existing field, permission and layout metadata can also render Salesforce through external AI interfaces; APIs predate MCP.

Agents may make buried enterprise information easier to use, while future interfaces adapt screens to conversation and incoming work. That dynamic-interface vision is a direction, not a universally shipped capability.
Build responsibility into company culture early rather than waiting for regulation. Benioff pairs growth with giving back and argues good products, accountability and philanthropy can coexist.

Pat Simmons launches four parallel one-shot builds to test Claude Opus 5.5 against Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra, then separates release claims from results. Opus 5.5 is priced at $4 per million input and $20 per million output tokens versus Opus 5's $5/$25; Anthropic's roughly 40% task-cost saving also assumes fewer tokens used. On the cited Terminal Bench, the scores are 66% for Opus, 55% for Fable and 57.9% for Astra; Frontier Code is closer at 54%, 50% and 53.3%. He notes Astra still leads an automation test, some comparison-table results are missing, and Anthropic itself says the real-world Opus–Fable gap may be narrower than the charts suggest.

For an Awwwards winner chosen separately by each agent, he blind-ranks Fable first, Opus second and Astra third, then checks their copies against the source sites. Opus recreates its site's scrolling and interactions closely but lacks project imagery; Fable's more polished-looking infrastructure site wins his subjective ranking even though its 3D interaction falls short of the original. Reported build costs and times are Opus $47/76 minutes, Fable $177/75 minutes and Astra $144/60 minutes: the cheapest here is not the winner.

The three agents next tackle the same animated yerba-mate site, including a Blender can and small jumping game. Opus wins for its coherent page, product shots and working game; Fable's can motion impresses but missing images and broken sections undermine the finished page. This time Opus costs $58 over 74 minutes, Fable $107 over 45 minutes and Astra $33 over 39 minutes. In a playable RollerCoaster Tycoon 2-style build, he again ranks Opus first for recognizable visuals and simpler ride-building; Astra's different-looking version is second, while Fable's controls are too confusing for him to fully test.

For a Blender-modeled Adidas shoe exploded into a product page, Astra has the most detailed shoe but the weakest page integration; the host nevertheless ranks it first, Opus second and Fable third. Reported shoe-run costs are Astra $13, Opus $33 and Fable $65, while Opus takes 91 minutes. Across the four subjective rankings Opus takes two firsts and two seconds, which makes it his default over Fable for most work at lower observed cost; he keeps Astra in play for 3D and reserves judgment on Fable for heavy, long-running coding. These are single-shot prompts and a handful of subjective builds, not proof of broad superiority or reliable total-cost savings on every task.
videos.why_valuable: [0:55–9:10] Connects per-token prices to benchmark and task-level efficiency rather than equating a cheaper token with a cheaper completed job. [9:10–33:58] Lets web/game/3D builders compare blind-ranked, visually inspected outputs alongside actual reported run costs and elapsed times: Opus wins both the shared brand-page and coaster tests, but Fable wins the first site and Astra the shoe. [33:58–35:06] The practical decision is to trial Opus as a default while retaining alternatives for specialized 3D or prolonged coding, and to replicate the prompts before budgeting from these small one-shot samples.
key_takeaways: [0:55–2:20] Opus 5.5 lists $4/$20 per million input/output tokens versus Opus 5's $5/$25; the roughly 40% saving is Anthropic's task-level estimate, not the raw price reduction.

[4:46–8:45] Cited Terminal Bench scores are Opus 66%, Fable 55%, Astra 57.9%; Frontier Code is Opus 54%, Fable 50%, Astra 53.3%. Astra leads one automation comparison, and not every benchmark has every model's result.
[9:10–17:47] The blind Awwwards-copy ranking is Fable > Opus > Astra; reported Opus/Fable/Astra costs are $47/$177/$144 and durations 76/75/60 minutes, respectively.

[17:47–24:48] For the same yerba-mate site, Opus places first with a working jumping mini-game; Fable has broken or absent images despite good can rotation. Opus takes 74 minutes/$58 versus Fable's 45 minutes/$107 and Astra's 39 minutes/$33.
[24:48–29:15] Opus wins the RollerCoaster Tycoon-style build on likeness and usable ride-building; Astra ranks second and Fable third, though the host does not exhaustively play-test the games.
[29:15–33:58] Astra's shoe model wins on 3D detail despite weak page integration; Opus is second. Shoe-test costs are $13 Astra, $33 Opus and $65 Fable; Opus takes 91 minutes.

[33:58–35:06] Verdict: Opus records two firsts and two seconds across four subjective single-shot trials and becomes the host's everyday default, but he still wants longer-running coding and dedicated 3D comparisons before generalizing.

chapters.title: Intro
chapters.description: Anthropic's new Opus 5.5 is framed as a response to GPT-6 Astra, with early benchmark gains that may even challenge Fable 5.1. The presenter sets up a practical comparison of quality, cost, and efficiency through four live projects: two website recreations, a browser game, and a 3D shoe embedded in a product page.

chapters.title: Kicking off the builds
chapters.description: A shell command launches separate agent windows so all four projects can run while the presenter examines the release. The parallel workloads include an award-winning website recreation, another branded site, a RollerCoaster Tycoon-style game, and an Adidas shoe modeled in Blender for display on a website.

chapters.title: Pricing
chapters.description: While the builds run, the presenter shows an interactive explainer made with Opus 5.5 and examines Anthropic's release page. Input and output prices fall to $4 and $20 per million tokens, respectively, versus $5 and $25 for Opus 5; lower cache costs and fewer tokens per completed task underpin Anthropic's claimed overall savings. He also discusses increased five-hour subscription limits after earlier confusion over a promotion, and highlights Anthropic's claim that the model communicates more concisely. Before turning to scores, he cautions that benchmark charts may overstate its advantage over Fable 5.1 in real work.

chapters.title: Benchmarks
chapters.description: The presenter walks through multi-step command-line coding, merge-worthy repository changes, Cursor coding, office work, automations, scientific questions, computer use, and chart reading. Opus 5.5 leads Fable 5.1 by a sizable margin on Terminal Bench and improves on several other measures, while its Frontier Code lead over Astra is narrow and Astra remains ahead on automation. He notes that automation failures can include Anthropic safety refusals, and questions why Astra's published computer-use score is absent from the comparison.

chapters.title: Tests missing from Anthropic's table
chapters.description: An additional comparison fills in omitted results, including a computer-use score that puts Opus 5.5 ahead of Astra, while marking 3D CAD and other tests for which the new model has no reported result. The presenter also examines Artificial Analysis rankings and effort-level breakdowns: Opus generally leads, but its Frontier Code result is strongest at medium effort rather than improving with more effort. These apparent advantages make it an attractive default on paper, setting up the question of whether the live builds agree.

chapters.title: Build 1: Awwwards clone
chapters.description: Using a website-cloning skill and a prompt to select and recreate an award-winning site, the presenter blindly reviews three outputs for animation, visual design, navigation, and usability. The most convincing overall design is revealed as Fable 5.1, while Opus 5.5's cleaner but simpler agency recreation closely matches its source when checked side by side; Astra's version is judged less successful. He compares each output with its actual reference site and then finds that Opus's roughly $47 build is far cheaper than Fable's roughly $177, despite Fable winning his aesthetic ranking.

chapters.title: Build 2: Yerba mate brand clone
chapters.description: All three agents attempt the same elaborate beverage website, including a Blender-generated can, scroll-driven rotations, branded sections, and a small jumping game. One version has strong can movement but missing images and broken sections; the best version combines convincing product visuals, text effects, scroll transitions, and a working game, although its can top and some icons still need refinement. The winner is Opus 5.5, ahead of Fable 5.1 and Astra; its roughly $58 run costs less than Fable's roughly $107 but takes substantially longer, while Astra is cheaper still.

chapters.title: Build 3: RollerCoaster Tycoon clone
chapters.description: The agents receive a prompt for a playable browser recreation with guidance on rendering, track construction, ride ratings, and park systems. In a hands-on review, one game has confusing track controls and rough graphics, another is easier to operate but barely resembles the original, and the strongest has more faithful scenery and straightforward ride-building tools. The reveal identifies Opus 5.5 as the clear winner, Astra second, and Fable 5.1 third, though the presenter acknowledges that asking for an empty starting map would have made all three easier to assess.

chapters.title: Build 4: Adidas shoe in Blender
chapters.description: Each model is asked to use shoe reference photography to create a detailed Blender model and place it in an interactive Adidas-style product page with component callouts and an exploded view. The first two pages handle scrolling and annotations reasonably well but miss shoe detail; the third has markedly better sole texture and upper detail, even though its page interaction and reassembly are weaker. That superior 3D model gives Astra first place, Opus 5.5 second, and Fable 5.1 third, with Astra also costing less and finishing faster than Opus in this test.

chapters.title: Final thoughts
chapters.description: Across the four one-shot trials, Opus 5.5 finishes first twice and second twice, making it the presenter's strongest overall option at much lower cost than Fable 5.1. He stresses that these limited runs do not settle performance on prolonged coding work, where he still intends to test Fable, or on 3D modeling, where Astra remains compelling. His practical plan is to default to Opus for most tasks, reserve comparisons with Fable for demanding long-running jobs, and investigate the models further in future builds.

quick_takeaways: Simmons chooses Opus 5.5 as his default over Fable for most work: it placed first twice and second twice across four subjective builds, generally at lower observed cost than Fable.
Fable won his blind Awwwards-site ranking, although its 3D interaction missed the original. Opus was cheaper at a reported $47 versus $177, showing that lowest cost and preferred design differ.

Opus won the animated yerba-mate page and RollerCoaster Tycoon-style game for coherent integration and usable controls. Inspect the finished flow, not only an impressive individual animation or asset.
Astra produced the most detailed Blender shoe and won that task despite weak page integration. Keep it in consideration for 3D rather than extending Opus's overall verdict to every specialty.
Reported token prices are $4/M input and $20/M output for Opus 5.5. Release claims of cheaper tasks depend on token use; actual time and spend varied substantially across prompts.

These are one-shot builds and personal rankings. Missing benchmark comparisons and a potentially narrower real-world Opus/Fable gap are reasons to test your own workload, especially long-running coding.

videos.description:
They’re revolutionising motoring, but what are the risks?  

Chinese electric vehicles are increasingly popular with Australian consumers. But this spike in EVs brings with it a new set of challenges.  

The vehicles’ cameras, microphones and constant connection to the internet could be problematic for personal privacy and national security. 

And while some cabinet ministers drive them, experts say Australia’s privacy and cybersecurity laws are leaving us exposed.  

On Four Corners this week, reporter Angus Grigg reveals just how much of your personal information can be seen by one Chinese EV, while exposing the potential for surveillance and even sabotage in another.

videos.summary:
Four Corners investigates the privacy and security of connected cars in Australia, focusing on Chinese EVs while explicitly noting that nearly all new cars transmit data. Researcher Dan Restchuk buys a BYD Shark 6 plug-in hybrid, locates camera connectors and taps its internal CAN bus. The report cites BYD's roughly 100,000 projected Australian vehicle sales that year and Chinese marques' more-than-half share of Australian EV sales; motoring journalist Samantha Stevens explains why the competitively priced XPeng G6 appeals to drivers despite privacy questions. Critics flag Chinese national-security law, but potential capability is not evidence of actual state use.

An XPeng insider uses ordinary manufacturer access, not a hack, to follow the reporter's real-time location, speed, steering and seat occupancy. Messages concerning a stolen XPeng prompt questions about remote shutdown; XPeng explicitly denies that it, China or a third party can remotely immobilize a customer vehicle. Separately, a log shows over-the-air software packages sent to Australian XPeng cars in March, including a battery-management-system package; the investigation raises concerns about scrutiny and transparency, without proving the updates malicious. Climate minister Chris Bowen, who drives a G6, says connected cars of all origins collect data and that he follows security advice. XPeng says it has neither provided Australian customer data to Chinese authorities nor received such a request.

After two weeks of research, Restchuk reports an unprotected access path on the BYD Shark 6 that did not even require a password. In a staged demonstration he remotely tracks the reporter, listens to a deliberately staged call containing clues to a temporary banking password, detects nearby Wi-Fi/Bluetooth networks and uses an unlocked phone left in the vehicle to query Siri for personal details. On a controlled road test at about 30 km/h, he triggers wipers and interferes with lights; he explicitly says he could not tamper with brakes or steering. The sequence demonstrates exploitable capability under this test setup, not that BYD or Chinese authorities performed these actions.

Home affairs minister Tony Burke says Australia has begun consulting on connected-vehicle rules but gives no timetable for minimum automotive cyber standards, even though consumer connected devices already face requirements. Privacy-law expert Katharine Kemp criticizes BYD's broad surveillance and disclosure language. The earlier privacy policy named China among 16 possible transfer countries; a newly posted version supplied after questions removed that and the surveillance wording. BYD says it stores the data in Australia and has not and would not transfer Australians' data to Chinese authorities; a policy change or legal possibility alone does not establish a transfer. Draft privacy-law reform is discussed.

Reporters count 22 EVs, almost half Chinese marques, in one car park near Australian intelligence and defence buildings. They contrast that access with China's past Tesla restrictions, UK military restrictions and Australia's 2023 removal of certain Chinese-made CCTV from federal premises. A Leapmotor's Dahua-labeled cameras prompt concern about passive observation near sensitive sites, although the film shows no resulting espionage. The closing verdict is that vehicle and privacy safeguards have lagged connected-car capabilities; the proposed remedy is risk-based controls on collection, software and sensitive-site access, not a claim that every Chinese EV is currently spying or sabotaging.
videos.why_valuable: [9:15–16:30] Shows buyers and fleet managers precisely what ordinary manufacturer access and remote updates can reveal or change, while retaining XPeng's denial about immobilization. [19:22–29:00] Distinguishes the BYD researcher's staged access and limited wiper/light demonstration from an uncontrolled exploit or proven espionage, making the threat model concrete without overstating it. [29:00–44:39] Gives security and privacy teams specific issues to assess before procurement: authentication, patch oversight, phone pairing, data-transfer clauses and rules for parking or driving near sensitive facilities.
key_takeaways: [2:07–4:37] The researcher buys a BYD Shark 6 plug-in hybrid and examines camera connections and CAN-bus traffic before testing remote-access weaknesses over two weeks.

[4:37–6:30] The report projects roughly 100,000 BYD Australian sales that year and says Chinese EVs exceed half of local EV sales; it also acknowledges data collection is common to nearly all new cars.

[9:15–13:50] An XPeng insider with manufacturer access reads location, speed, steering angle and occupancy in real time. A stolen-car discussion raises shutdown concerns, but XPeng denies having remote immobilization capability.

[14:00–16:30] A March log shows over-the-air XPeng software updates to Australian cars, including a battery-management package; the report questions absent Australian review, not proof of malicious code.

[19:22–28:55] The BYD researcher finds a passwordless access path, stages microphone and location surveillance, and triggers wipers and lights in a low-speed test. He says brakes and steering were not tampered with; the phone-based Siri probe requires a phone left unlocked inside.

[29:00–34:40] Australia has no minimum automotive cyber standard in the report; BYD's older policy named China among 16 potential data destinations, while a new policy removes the reference. BYD denies sending Australian customer data to Chinese authorities.

[36:40–43:40] Reporters count 22 EVs near intelligence and defence buildings, almost half Chinese marques, and identify Dahua-labeled cameras on a Leapmotor; proximity and hardware are risk indicators, not evidence that surveillance occurred.

[43:40–44:39] Verdict: experts call for stronger vehicle cybersecurity and privacy protections; the investigation demonstrates access and plausible misuse, not actual foreign-government control of these cars.

chapters.title: Intro
chapters.description: The film contrasts the privacy of older, largely disconnected cars with modern vehicles that carry cameras, microphones and persistent internet connections. It acknowledges the appeal and rapid growth of Chinese electric vehicles while previewing an investigation into manufacturer access, a security researcher's experiments and the gap in Australian regulation.

chapters.title: EV research project
chapters.description: Cybersecurity researcher Dan Restchuk brings a BYD Shark 6 plug-in hybrid into a garage to investigate what its cameras and internal systems could reveal or permit remotely. He identifies rear-camera connectors and taps the vehicle's CAN bus, where components exchange messages that can help him work out how to address lights and door locks. Despite liking the vehicle, he says its convenience can obscure security concerns and gives himself several weeks to test it.

chapters.title: Who are BYD?
chapters.description: BYD's rapid expansion has brought it close to Australia's leading car brands, backed by its own vehicle-shipping fleet and a projected roughly 100,000 local sales this year. The investigation notes that data collection is common across new cars, but focuses on Chinese EVs because they account for more than half of Australian EV sales and their software operators are subject to Chinese data-disclosure laws.

chapters.title: Why a Chinese EV has potential data risks?
chapters.description: Opposition defence spokesman James Paterson argues that Chinese national-security law can compel automakers to assist intelligence agencies, while Australia has not set limits on what their connected vehicles collect, store or transmit. He distinguishes the demonstrated capacity for surveillance or harm from any proven intention to use it, as the report moves toward testing another Chinese brand on Australian roads.

chapters.title: Reviewing a XPeng G6
chapters.description: Rally champion and motoring journalist Samantha Stevens drives the XPeng G6 and praises its acceleration, handling and braking despite its weight. She attributes the appeal of Chinese EVs to fast development, improving quality and lower prices, while saying buyers tend to notice features and cost more than privacy. XPeng's Australian launch ambitions provide the backdrop, although the program was not allowed to film its Melbourne brand event.

chapters.title: XPeng data harvesting
chapters.description: An XPeng insider uses ordinary manufacturer access, not a hack, to show live vehicle location, speed, steering angle, seat occupancy and driving inputs while the reporter travels through Sydney. Internal messages about a stolen car raise questions about remote intervention, but XPeng says it cannot remotely immobilise customers' vehicles and denies such a capability exists in China or elsewhere. Update logs then show software can be pushed from China into Australian cars, potentially without owners' express knowledge; experts warn these opaque updates can change safety-relevant behaviour, while Australia does not review them as China does.

chapters.title: Chris Bowen on his XPeng
chapters.description: Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen says he enjoys driving his XPeng and sees cheaper running costs and lower emissions as reasons to welcome growing EV adoption. Challenged about the manufacturer's access to his location, home address and vehicle status, he responds that connectivity affects many modern cars and says he follows security advice. A former cyber adviser warns that cabinet members and other sensitive personnel are especially attractive intelligence targets; XPeng says it has never supplied Australian customer data to Chinese authorities or received a request for it.

chapters.title: Hacking the BYD
chapters.description: After two weeks examining the BYD Shark's code, Dan Restchuk reports that he gained access more easily than expected through weaknesses that included an interface without a password. He contrasts this with Tesla's public bug-bounty and researcher programs, noting that BYD's Chinese vulnerability-reporting portal requires a Chinese mobile number. The segment ends with his offer to demonstrate what the access means during a drive rather than merely describing the flaw.

chapters.title: Surveillance risk
chapters.description: During a BYD Shark drive, Dan remotely tracks the reporter and activates its microphone to listen to a staged phone conversation containing clues to a temporary banking password. He also observes nearby Wi-Fi and Bluetooth access points, which could map networks around a route. After recording the reporter's voice, he replays it through the car's speakers to query an unlocked phone's voice assistant for personal details and a contact number, demonstrating a chain of exposure beyond simple location tracking.

chapters.title: Sabotage risk
chapters.description: On an isolated road after dark, Dan has the reporter drive slowly while he operates a laptop from the roadside. He says he cannot interfere with braking or steering, but remotely switches on the windscreen wipers and manipulates the headlights, ultimately turning the lights off. The controlled demonstration shows how access to less critical vehicle functions could still create a serious driving hazard.

chapters.title: Why don’t we have minimum cyber security laws around vehicles in Australia?
chapters.description: Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke is pressed on why Australia has minimum cybersecurity rules for some household connected devices but not for cars travelling at highway speeds. He says the government started with simpler, commonly attacked devices, declines to give a timetable for vehicle standards and points to consultation on new rules. The report then pivots from technical security standards to troubling terms in BYD's Australian privacy policy.

chapters.title: BYD privacy policy
chapters.description: Privacy-law scholar Katherine Kemp rejects BYD's reassuring opening language as no substitute for meaningful protections. Asked to examine the company's Australian policy, she identifies broad terms governing the use of personal information, including a reference to surveillance activities. Her assessment sets up a closer examination of where Australian drivers' data might be sent and how freely it could be disclosed.

chapters.title: Personal data of Australians going to China
chapters.description: Katherine Kemp finds that BYD's policy gave it broad discretion to collect and disclose personal information and listed China among possible destinations; after the program questioned the company, a newly uploaded policy removed references to China and surveillance. BYD says it stores Australian data locally and has not transferred it to Chinese authorities, although the report notes overseas transfer remains possible and Chinese law may require company cooperation. The discussion broadens to limits on meaningful consumer consent, proposed Australian privacy-law reform and restrictions on connected vehicles near sensitive facilities in China and the UK, contrasted with Australia's less explicit approach.

chapters.title: How many EVs parked near high security buildings
chapters.description: The reporter surveys a Canberra car park near major security agencies and identifies BYDs, other Chinese marques and several Teslas among the parked vehicles. The team counts 22 electric vehicles, nearly half of them Chinese brands, beside the Australian Signals Directorate headquarters. The location turns an abstract question about sensitive sites into a visible example of connected cars sitting near intelligence infrastructure.

chapters.title: Chinese security cameras banned from federal buildings
chapters.description: With intelligence and defence offices nearby, the report recalls Australia's removal of Chinese-made CCTV from federal buildings in 2023 over surveillance concerns. It traces one affected manufacturer, Dahua, to cameras identified in Leapmotor vehicles, explaining that the company was also sanctioned over its role in surveillance of Uyghurs in Xinjiang. Unlike cameras installed inside government buildings, the same manufacturer's cameras in connected cars face no comparable restriction as the vehicles pass sensitive sites.

chapters.title: Dangers of Chinese EVs near sensitive buildings
chapters.description: Former cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon rides in a six-camera Leapmotor and explains how repeated passes or parking near government offices could reveal staff movements, work patterns and activity at sensitive buildings. Police question the crew when they film across from an intelligence site, sharpening the contrast with a camera-equipped car that could remain nearby. The report argues for broader rules on vehicle data collection, storage and transmission, while experts distinguish a plausible surveillance capability from proof that it is being used.

chapters.title: Would this privacy expert buy a connected vehicle?
chapters.description: Katherine Kemp says she has delayed buying a new car because she lacks confidence in manufacturers' data handling and the enforcement of Australian privacy law. The closing narration argues that vehicle regulation and older privacy protections have not kept pace with connected technology. It returns to the contrast with simpler, unconnected motoring while acknowledging that such an era cannot be restored.

quick_takeaways: Connected-car data collection is widespread across origins. Four Corners shows ordinary XPeng manufacturer access exposing live location, speed, steering and seat occupancy; a hack was not needed for that access.

A researcher found an unprotected BYD access path and demonstrated tracking, staged-call listening and nearby-network detection. An unlocked phone left inside also exposed personal information through Siri.

In a controlled low-speed test he interfered with lights and wipers, but explicitly could not alter brakes or steering. Demonstrated access is not evidence that a manufacturer or government used it maliciously.

Over-the-air updates and broad privacy policies deserve scrutiny. BYD changed policy wording after questions and says Australian data stays in Australia; XPeng denies remote customer-vehicle immobilization and government data transfers.
Australia's automotive cyber standards were still under consultation without a timetable in the report. Privacy safeguards and software transparency had lagged vehicle connectivity.

Evaluate collection, disclosure, update controls and access near sensitive sites. Legal possibilities and cameras create potential risk, but the documentary does not establish actual state espionage or sabotage.

videos.summary:
Theo contrasts Elon Musk's promises of superior real-world coding and token efficiency for Grok 4.7 with what he sees in agentic workloads. After a clearly marked Blacksmith CI sponsorship, he cites Artificial Analysis task totals of about 38,000 tokens for Grok 4.6 versus 81,000 for 4.7. He argues a Cursor executive's production figures of only 5% more tokens per median request and 20–30% more at the 99th percentile do not settle per-task economics: one prompt can spawn many tool-call requests. Those production and benchmark measurements have different scopes, and his explanation of the discrepancy is an inference rather than internal proof.

In the creator's codebase-test runs one Grok attempt would cost about $20 at API rates, versus the next costliest Astra run at $11.44. He reviews the company's mixed selection of Cursor Bench, software, electrical and legal benchmarks, a strong Briefcase result and weak Terminal Bench relative to Fable. Frontier Code can fluctuate with reasoning effort, and the company says Grok 4.7 sometimes overcooks patches, so he rejects any single leaderboard as decisive. Artificial Analysis's coding-agent index gives Grok Build 56 versus 62 for leading alternatives; he sees a real supervision gap despite some task-specific strengths. Grok 4.7's full benchmark task cost is quoted at $3.74 against Astra's $3.26, despite unchanged headline token pricing versus Grok 4.6.

A Grok-friendly colleague reports $40 of usage consuming 8% of a $300/month plan's weekly allowance; the creator also notes higher rates past a 200,000-token context and for fast mode. Artificial Analysis places Grok near the front on AA Briefcase but reports worse presentation quality than 4.6. He shows poor front-end examples, an agent trapped in self-congratulatory repetitive output and a strange X translation. These are illustrations of failure modes, not frequency estimates; he speculates that additional last-minute reinforcement learning to discourage early quitting contributed to extra tokens.

Theo still likes Grok 4.7's tendency to stay on task and investigate code deeply. In his exploratory T3 Code codebase audit, Fable 5.1 and Astra judges place Grok's improvement suggestions just behind Astra for viability and ahead of Fable's smaller set, but repeated checking can drive its worst-case run to roughly twice the cost of Astra or Fable. With the same prompt and environment, his Fish Slop game run takes nearly 90 minutes and looks markedly worse than Astra's, including broken movement and weak fish and submarine visuals. Verdict: interesting and sometimes useful for codebase investigation, especially for existing Cursor users, but not a general recommendation at current cost, speed and subscription limits; his ad hoc audit and demo are not controlled evidence of universal model quality.
videos.why_valuable: [3:30–8:00] Gives agent users a practical accounting rule: compare completed-task token use and cost, not just per-request averages or advertised price per million tokens. [12:00–18:00] Places selected release benchmarks beside independent coding-agent results and reported context/subscription charges. [21:30–27:53] Separates a genuinely useful codebase-audit behavior from a poor same-prompt game demo, helping decide whether to pilot Grok for investigative repository work rather than migrate an entire coding workflow based on one score.
key_takeaways: [3:30–7:55] Artificial Analysis task counts cited are about 38,000 tokens for Grok 4.6 and 81,000 for 4.7; Cursor's 5% median and 20–30% P99 increases measure tokens per request, not necessarily per completed agent task.
[7:20–8:00] In the host's codebase test, his most expensive Grok 4.7 run would cost about $20 at API rates, compared with $11.44 for the next most expensive Astra run.

[10:00–14:45] Official benchmarks are mixed: Grok is strong on some specialty tasks and Briefcase but trails Fable on Terminal Bench; Artificial Analysis's coding-agent index scores Grok Build 56 versus 62 for the leading agents.
[14:45–16:45] Artificial Analysis task cost is quoted as $3.74 for Grok 4.7 versus $3.26 for Astra; same advertised price per token as Grok 4.6 does not guarantee same task-level bill.

[16:00–17:10] Reported Grok pricing rises beyond 200,000 tokens and in fast mode; a colleague says $40 of usage depleted 8% of his $300/month plan's weekly quota, one user's experience rather than a universal quota calculation.
[19:00–21:30] A showcased agent loops on grandiose text and an X translation leaks odd formatting; anecdotes flag quality-control issues but do not measure how often they happen.
[21:30–24:10] An ad hoc T3 Code audit yields Grok suggestions rated just behind Astra for viability by Fable/Astra judges, but excessive verification can make a run roughly twice as costly.

[24:10–27:53] The same-prompt Fish Slop build takes almost 90 minutes and falls short of Astra's result. Verdict: promising investigator, weak value as a general coding default at these prices; both demos are limited samples.

chapters.title: Grok 4.7’s Promise Meets the Token Bill
chapters.description: The host opens with Elon’s ambitious coding claims for Grok 4.7, then argues that benchmark scores miss what makes the model useful in practice. After a Blacksmith sponsorship about faster, cheaper GitHub Actions runners, he compares the release’s promised efficiency with Artificial Analysis token counts and costs. He questions whether production figures measured per request can meaningfully answer a benchmark measuring whole tasks, especially when agentic prompts trigger multiple tool calls.

chapters.title: Agent Costs and a Patchwork of Benchmarks
chapters.description: The per-request distinction leads into the host’s own costly Grok 4.7 runs, where more requests and tokens can make a complete task far pricier than its listed token rate suggests. He works through the official Cursor Bench and specialist results, noting both genuine strengths and awkward comparisons with Fable, Astra, and other models. He then questions the release’s selective charts, the noisy Frontier Code results, and Grok’s weak position on Artificial Analysis despite improvements to its agent-focused index.

chapters.title: Coding-Agent Gaps, Pricing Limits, and Strange Loops
chapters.description: Artificial Analysis’s coding-agent index puts Grok Build below the leading agents, a gap the host says translates into more supervision even on ordinary work. He and a Grok-enthusiast colleague also find that heavy token use, long-context charges, and fast-mode pricing erode the generous subscription value older Grok models offered. A strong Briefcase showing contrasts with poor front-end examples, while discussion of last-minute reinforcement learning culminates in an example of the model looping through grandiose claims instead of finishing its task.

chapters.title: A Useful Codebase Audit, a Bad Fish Demo, and the Verdict
chapters.description: After showing a bizarre translation output on X, the host explains why he still likes Grok 4.7: it stays on task and digs deeply enough to find useful codebase improvements. His T3 Code audit places its suggestions near the top for viability, but repeated verification can double the cost, and a Fish Slop build takes nearly ninety minutes yet looks much worse than the same prompt run with Astra. He concludes that the model is an interesting stepping stone rather than a recommendation at its current price, speed, and subscription limits.

quick_takeaways: Compare cost per completed agent task, not per token or median request. One prompt can trigger many tool calls; Theo argues Grok 4.7's extra investigation can make unchanged token rates misleading.

He finds Grok persistent and sometimes useful for codebase audits, with viable suggestions close behind Astra in his exploratory review. That strength comes with supervision and worst-case cost concerns.
His quoted codebase-test run was about $20 API equivalent versus the next-highest Astra run at $11.44. Check allowance consumption and higher rates beyond 200K context or in fast mode.
Inspect patch scope and stop repetitive loops. The company acknowledges occasional overcooked patches, while Theo shows self-congratulatory repetition and weak frontend examples.
His Fish Slop build took nearly 90 minutes and had broken movement and poor visuals. Deep investigation did not translate into a good game or polished presentation in that run.

He sees a possible fit for existing Cursor users doing investigation, rather than a general recommendation. Benchmarks, production request statistics and his demos measure different things and should not be treated as interchangeable.

videos.title: You Eat the Fruit of Your Theology — Russell Johnson on Mature Me Ep 107
videos.description:
Is the Holy Spirit welcome or is He needed in your life?

This week on Mature Me, I sit down with my friend @russellbjohnson lead pastor of @ThePursuitNW, for a conversation about bold faith and what it means to stay dependent on God.

We go after the things we want in life, but when it comes to our faith, we can settle for being open. Open to a miracle. Open to God moving. But are we pursuing Him? Are we praying with expectation and taking steps that require us to trust Him?

As we mature, our dependence on God should deepen. More experience, more opportunity, and more responsibility should keep bringing us back to the same place: we need Him.

We can be grateful for what God has done and still be hungry for more.

Tune in tonight at 7:30 PM on the Rich Wilkerson Jr. YouTube Channel. 🔗

Stay tuned to all of Rich’s latest content: https://www.richwilkersonjr.com

Listen to this episode on Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/show/5irnf5xVweBzylMB7L12lM?si=c1fa4ecc659e420e&nd=1&dlsi=9ee25cfb9b234d11

Listen to this episode on Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/mature-me-w-rich-wilkerson-jr/id1727468541

Follow Rich on Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/richwilkersonjr/
Follow Rich on TikTok: https://www.tiktok.com/@richwilkersonjr?lang=en


Chapters
0:00 Faith Is for What You Can’t Do
9:40 What’s Different About the Pacific Northwest?
15:00 The Environment That Shapes Your Faith
20:00 Great Churches Don’t Happen by Accident
25:00 Why Discontentment Can Spark Revival
34:20 Are We Desperate Enough for God?
43:30 What Does Revival Actually Look Like?
52:00 When Church Becomes Too Comfortable
1:00:30 Give God a Problem Worth Solving
1:09:00 Stop Playing It Safe With Your Faith
1:13:49 Russell's VOUSCon Offering Talk
1:22:10 What's Your Favorite Place to Preach?
